newsitem.title: UK: UK minister Donoughue greets EU farm reform moves.
newsitem.headline: UK minister Donoughue greets EU farm reform moves.

text.p: EU plans for the reform of the common agricultural policy have been welcomed by Britain's food industry minister Lord Donoughue.
"We think it is a welcome step in the right direction," he said, speaking to the Home grown Cereals Authority's annual harvest lunch.
"The broad drift of the paper is in line with the broad drift of our approach," he said.
The European Commission on Wednesday published proposals for further price cutting farm reforms that it says are needed to prepare for EU expansion eastwards and to prevent food surpluses returning.

The Agenda 2000 proposals, which were approved on Tuesday, include dairy, cereals and beef intervention price cuts of 10, 20 and 30 percent respectively and would be partially compensated by direct income payments.
"Reform is essential," Donoughue said. The only viable way ahead was through reductions in support prices.
Along with the reform of the CAP, the priority of the new Labour government, elected in May, was to restore consumer confidence through the establishment of a food standards agency, he said.
The ministry of agriculture was already working closely with the department of health and the government was promoting consumer consciousness within the farm ministry.

Donoughue expressed recognition of farmers' concerns over the strength of sterling and the revaluation of the green pound. But he noted that arable area payments, the compensation paid to farmers for the effects of the 1992 reform of the CAP, were "substantially protected."

Britain's Home Grown Cereals Authority chairman Brian Nelson noted that sterling's recent strength had only brought it back to rates which were expected at the time the 1992 reform was agreed. "The industry has lost that insulation," he said, referring to the lower rates which have prevailed since the reform.
